rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Evolution is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Homologous organs (common origin, divergent function), analogous organs (convergent evolution), and vestigial structures reveal common ancestry. Fossils document the progressive increase in complexity and transitional forms like Archaeopteryx.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Homologous: same structure, different function, common origin (divergent evolution)
Analogous: different structure, same function, different origin (convergent evolution)
Vestigial: reduced remnant of an ancestral organ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Homologous = same origin, different function (divergent); Analogous = different origin, same function (convergent).  ·  Vestigial organs are evidence of common ancestry, not of "uselessness" in an absolute sense.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB frequently asks for homologous vs analogous organs with examples.  ·  Vestigial organs in humans (appendix, coccyx) are a common short-answer.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Homologous: forelimbs of human (arm), bat (wing), whale (flipper), horse (leg) — same bone pattern, different use.  ·  Analogous: wings of bird (feather, bone) vs insect (chitin, no bone) — both fly, different origin.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Fossils are not just "old bones"; they include traces (footprints, burrows), impressions, and molecular fossils.  ·  Archaeopteryx shows both reptilian (teeth, long bony tail, claws) and avian (feathers, wing) features — a transitional form.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Differentiate homologous vs analogous  ·  List 3 vestigial organs

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Homo = same origin; Ana = same function.  ·  Vestigial = "Vest" (a leftover vest of evolution).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: How do homologous organs support evolution?  ·  Differentiate homologous from analogous organs.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Differentiate homologous and analogous organs (with examples).  ·  Explain vestigial organs as evidence of evolution.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Homologous vs analogous  ·  Vestigial organs  ·  Fossil evidence  ·  Archaeopteryx

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Five types of evidence: morphological, anatomical, fossil, embryological, biochemical.  ·  Homologous (divergent) vs analogous (convergent) organs.  ·  Vestigial organs = reduced ancestral remnants.  ·  Fossils show progressive complexity; transitional forms link groups.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Archaeopteryx lithographica (1861, Germany) is the classic bird-reptile transitional fossil.  ·  Humans and chimpanzees share ~98.8% of their DNA.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What are vestigial organs and why are they evidence of evolution?  ·  Explain the significance of Archaeopteryx.  ·  How does the molecular/cytoplasmic evidence (DNA, proteins) support evolution?

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Describe the significance of Archaeopteryx.  ·  State the embryological evidence for evolution.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Vestigial: human appendix, coccyx (tailbone), wisdom teeth; whale pelvic bones.  ·  Transitional: Archaeopteryx; Tiktaalik (fish-amphibian link); Australopithecus (human ancestor).

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The wings of a bat and the wings of a bird are: → B  ·  Archaeopteryx is significant because it: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Evidence of evolution: morphological, anatomical, paleontological (fossil), embryological, and biochemical/molecular.  ·  Homologous organs (divergent evolution): similar structure, different function, common ancestry — e.g. forelimbs of whale, bat, human, horse.  ·  Analogous organs (convergent evolution): similar function, different structure/origin — e.g. wings of bird vs insect; eyes of octopus vs vertebrate.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Embryological evidence  ·  Molecular evidence  ·  Universal genetic code

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Molecular clock  ·  Molecular: DNA/protein similarity inversely related to evolutionary distance  ·  Embryos of vertebrates are similar early, diverge later.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Universal genetic code + similar proteins (cytochrome c) = molecular evidence.  ·  Molecular clock estimates divergence time.  ·  Embryological similarity reflects common ancestry; the differences develop later as embryos mature.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A "universal genetic code" (same codons → same amino acids) across all life is strong evidence of common descent.  ·  Molecular: cytochrome c in horse vs human differs by only a few amino acids.  ·  Archaeopteryx as a transitional fossil is a very frequent exam topic.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Molecular evidence (DNA similarity, cytochrome c) is increasingly tested.  ·  Memorise 2 homologous and 2 analogous examples.  ·  List 3 vestigial organs in humans.
